title: Internet Providers in Seattle, WA: 14 ISPs Compared
description: Internet providers in Seattle, WA: Xfinity, Quantum Fiber (now AT&T), Astound, Ziply, 5G and satellite across 41 ZIP codes, plus cheapest and low-income plans.
lead: Every ISP reporting service in Seattle's 41 ZIP codes, how cable, fiber and 5G compare here, the cheapest plans, and the city's low-income options.
short_answer: Xfinity cable and Quantum Fiber, now owned by AT&T, both report service in all 41 Seattle ZIP codes in June 2026 FCC data. Astound offers cable and fiber in 24 of them, and Ziply Fiber only on the north edge. Verizon, T-Mobile and AT&T 5G home internet cover the city, and low-income plans start near $10 a month.

sections.h2: Every provider reporting service in Seattle (41 ZIP codes)

sections.body_html: Source: FCC Broadband Data Collection, June 30, 2026, matched to ZIP codes by YourBillCheck. "ZIP codes served" counts the 41 ZIP codes with a Seattle postal address where each provider reports any service, so it includes a few areas outside city limits and is a guide, not a promise for your street.

sections.h2: Cable, fiber or 5G: how Seattle's networks compare
sections.body_html:
Cable: Xfinity is the one wired network almost every Seattle home can get. In the FCC data it reports cable in all 41 ZIP codes, covering most of the area in each, with top speeds of 2 Gbps. BroadbandNow puts Xfinity's Seattle coverage at about 97%. Astound also runs cable, mostly south of the Ship Canal and Lake Union, from Queen Anne and Capitol Hill down to Georgetown and the Rainier Valley, according to BroadbandNow.

Fiber: Quantum Fiber, now owned by AT&T, reports fiber in all 41 ZIP codes, covering most of the area in 13 of them and a large part in most of the rest. BroadbandNow reports its coverage is strong in West Seattle, Delridge, Rainier Beach, Columbia City, most of Capitol Hill, Queen Anne, Magnolia and north of the University of Washington, and limited in Georgetown, SoDo, Downtown and Belltown. Astound reports fiber in parts of 22 ZIP codes, Ziply Fiber in 3 on the north edge, and Ezee Fiber in a small part of 98198. For plans and prices on each fiber network, see our fiber internet in Seattle guide.

5G home internet: Verizon, T-Mobile and AT&T all report fixed wireless in every Seattle ZIP code. Verizon reports the highest top speed, up to 1 Gbps. T-Mobile reaches most of the area in 33 of the 41 ZIP codes and Verizon in 24; AT&T reaches a smaller share, under 60% of each ZIP code. 5G is a fair choice for renters or light users, but speeds depend on signal at your home.

Apartments: Seattle IT also lists Atlas Networks and GFiber as providers that serve apartment and condo buildings, and Salmon Bay Wireless as a wireless option. Ask your building manager which providers are wired in before you sign a lease.

sections.h2: Who's who: CenturyLink, Quantum, AT&T, Wave, Astound and Ziply
sections.body_html:
1. Quantum Fiber is now AT&T. AT&T closed its $5.75 billion purchase of Lumen's consumer fiber business, including Quantum Fiber, on February 2, 2026, and named Seattle as one of its new major metro areas. In July 2026 AT&T said it was converting former Lumen fiber customers market by market; some still got CenturyLink or Quantum Fiber bills. Lumen kept its copper-based consumer services. CenturyLink DSL still appears separately in the FCC data, in 39 Seattle ZIP codes at up to 140 Mbps.
  2. Astound is the old Wave. Wave Broadband started in the Seattle area and was based in Kirkland. It took the Astound Broadband name in January 2022. In March 2026 Stonepeak and Alphabet agreed to combine Astound with GFiber (Google Fiber), with closing expected in the fourth quarter of 2026. GFiber's CEO said the merger will not affect current service.
  3. Ziply Fiber is based in Kirkland and was bought by Canada's BCE in August 2025. In Seattle it reports fiber only in 98177, 98133 and 98155.
  4. Webpass reports fixed wireless at up to 1 Gbps in a small part of six Seattle ZIP codes in the FCC data.

If your bill comes from one of these companies, see the AT&T bill guide, CenturyLink bill guide or Xfinity bill guide.

No. Seattle studied building its own gigabit fiber network. A 2015 consultant's study, reported by GeekWire, put the cost at $480 million to $665 million and said it would need 43% of single-family homes to subscribe at $75 a month to break even. City officials called that too risky to fund alone. Seattle City Light, which was already building its own fiber system, told the city that adding a broadband service would not make sense. Today the city's role is information and discount programs, not running an ISP.

sections.h2: What to ask before you sign up
sections.body_html:
1. Is my address on fiber or cable? Astound serves some homes by fiber and others by coax, and Quantum/AT&T fiber does not reach every street.
  2. What is the price after the promotion, and is there a price lock?
  3. Is there a data allowance, install fee or equipment charge?
  4. For 5G: what speed does my exact address get, and is there a trial period?

Run a speed test on your current plan first. If your bill has crept up, read why your internet bill went up and our guide to internet fees.

faq: What is the main internet provider in Seattle?

Xfinity cable is the most widely available wired network, covering most of the area in all 41 Seattle ZIP codes in June 2026 FCC data. Quantum Fiber, now owned by AT&T, also reports service in all 41, covering most of the area in 13 and a large part in most of the rest.
What is the cheapest internet in Seattle?

Among standard plans, Astound lists 300 Mbps from $30 a month and AT&T Fiber lists 300 Mbps at $35 a month for 12 months. Low-income households may qualify for Astound Internet First at $9.95 a month or Xfinity Internet Essentials at $14.95 a month.
Is Quantum Fiber the same as AT&T Fiber in Seattle?
Yes, it is now the same company. AT&T bought Lumen's consumer fiber business, including Quantum Fiber, on February 2, 2026, and is moving customers to the AT&T Fiber brand market by market.
Is Astound the same as Wave in Seattle?
Yes. Wave Broadband, founded in the Seattle area, took the Astound Broadband name in 2022. Astound agreed in March 2026 to combine with GFiber, with the deal expected to close in late 2026.

No. A 2015 city study put the cost of a city-built fiber network at $480 million to $665 million, and officials judged it too risky to build alone. The city runs low-cost internet sign-ups and information instead.
